templates.pattern: An electron in a hydrogen atom is in energy level n = [N]. Calculate the energy of the electron in eV using the Bohr model. (En = −13.6 ÷ n² eV)
templates.explanation:
Energy of electron = −13.6 ÷ n²
= −13.6 ÷ [N]²
= −13.6 ÷ [N*N]
= [RESULT] eV

The negative sign indicates the electron is bound to the nucleus. Energy level n=1 is the ground state with the most negative — most stable — energy. Higher levels are less negative — less stable.

templates.pattern: An electron in hydrogen falls from energy level n = [N2] to n = [N1]. Calculate the energy of the photon emitted in eV. (En = −13.6 ÷ n² eV)
templates.explanation:
Energy of photon = E_lower − E_upper
= −13.6/[N1]² − (−13.6/[N2]²)
= 13.6 × (1/[N1]² − 1/[N2]²)
= 13.6 × (1/[N1*N1] − 1/[N2*N2])
= [RESULT] eV

When an electron falls to a lower energy level it emits a photon. The photon energy equals the difference between the two energy levels. This produces the characteristic emission spectrum of hydrogen.

templates.pattern: A photon has a frequency of [F] × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the energy of the photon in joules. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
Photon energy E = hf
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × [F] × 10¹⁴
= 6.63 × [F] × 10⁻²⁰
= [RESULT] J

Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency. Ultraviolet photons have enough energy to cause chemical reactions and damage DNA. This is why UV radiation is harmful.

templates.pattern: A photon has an energy of [E] × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the wavelength of the photon in metres. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
From E = hc ÷ λ:
λ = hc ÷ E
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸ ÷ ([E] × 10⁻¹⁹)
= 19.89 × 10⁻²⁶ ÷ [E] × 10⁻¹⁹
= [RESULT] m

Visible light has wavelengths between 400 nm and 700 nm. This formula connects the particle nature (energy) and wave nature (wavelength) of light.

templates.pattern: An electron of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg moves at [V] × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in metres. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ mv
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × [V] × 10⁶)
= 6.63 ÷ (9.11 × [V] × 10³)
= [RESULT] m

The de Broglie wavelength shows that particles have wave properties. Electron diffraction experiments confirm this — electrons produce diffraction patterns just like waves.

templates.pattern: An atom has atomic number [Z] and a shielding constant of [S]. Calculate the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electrons.
templates.explanation:
Effective nuclear charge Z_eff = Z − σ
= [Z] − [S]
= [RESULT]

Inner shell electrons shield outer electrons from the full attraction of the nucleus. A larger effective nuclear charge means outer electrons are held more tightly — higher ionisation energy and smaller atomic radius.

templates.pattern: The successive ionisation energies of an element are [IE1], [IE2], [IE3] and [IE4] kJ/mol respectively. A large jump occurs between the [JUMP]th and [JUMP1]th values. In which group of the periodic table is this element?
templates.explanation:
A large jump in successive ionisation energies occurs when an electron is removed from an inner shell.
The large jump is between IE[JUMP] and IE[JUMP1].
This means [JUMP] electrons are in the outer shell.
Therefore the element is in Group [RESULT].

This is one of the most powerful tools for determining group number from ionisation energy data.

templates.pattern: The first ionisation energy of an element is [IE] kJ/mol. Calculate the energy needed in joules to ionise one atom of this element. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Energy per atom = ionisation energy ÷ Avogadro's number
= [IE] × 10³ J/mol ÷ 6.02 × 10²³
= [RESULT] J

Ionisation energies are usually quoted per mole. Dividing by Avogadro's number gives the energy needed to remove one electron from one atom.

templates.pattern: Two isotopes of an element have masses [M1] and [M2] with abundances [AB1]% and [AB2]% respectively. Calculate the relative atomic mass of the element.
templates.explanation:
RAM = (M₁ × AB₁% + M₂ × AB₂%) ÷ 100
= ([M1] × [AB1] + [M2] × [AB2]) ÷ 100
= ([M1*AB1] + [M2*AB2]) ÷ 100
= [RESULT]

Note this is a multi-isotope weighted average. This is why the periodic table shows non-integer values for relative atomic masses.

templates.pattern: A sample contains [N] × 10²³ atoms of element X (RAM = [RAM]). Calculate the mass of the sample in grams. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Moles = number of atoms ÷ Avogadro's number
= [N] × 10²³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³
= [N] ÷ 6.02 mol

Mass = moles × RAM
= ([N] ÷ 6.02) × [RAM]
= [RESULT] g

This connects the microscopic world of atoms to the macroscopic world of measurable masses.
